title: Java Generics Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Fast night-before revision of Java generics: type parameters, generic methods, bounds, wildcards with PECS, type erasure and its consequences, raw types and generic arrays.

chapters.title: Generics Mental Model
points: Generics add compile-time type safety: List<String> rejects add(42) at compile time and removes casts on get()
Type parameter conventions: T type, E element, K key, V value, N number; a generic class is declared class Box<T> { T val; }
Generic method declares its own parameter before the return type: static <T> T first(List<T> l); type usually inferred from arguments
Type arguments must be reference types: List<int> is illegal, use List<Integer> (autoboxing applies)
Generics are invariant: List<Integer> is NOT a List<Number> even though Integer extends Number; only the raw/wildcard forms relate them

chapters.title: Bounded Types and Wildcards
points: Upper bound on a type parameter: <T extends Comparable<T>> lets you call compareTo on T; multiple bounds use & with the class first: <T extends Number & Comparable<T>>
Unbounded wildcard List<?> means list of unknown type: you can read as Object but can only add null
Upper-bounded wildcard List<? extends Number> is read-only (producer): reads give Number, add() of anything except null fails to compile
Lower-bounded wildcard List<? super Integer> is write-friendly (consumer): you can add Integer, reads give only Object
PECS (Producer Extends, Consumer Super): Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src); use ? when you don't need the type name, T when the type links params or return

chapters.title: Type Erasure Internals
points: Erasure: the compiler removes type arguments after checking; T becomes its bound (or Object) and casts are inserted at call sites
Bytecode of List<String> and List<Integer> is the same class: List.class is shared, so getClass() on both is equal
Bridge methods: compiler generates synthetic methods to keep overriding working after erasure, e.g. compareTo(Object) calling compareTo(String)
Heap pollution: mixing raw and generic types lets a wrong element in, and the failure appears later as a ClassCastException at the cast the compiler inserted
Reification contrast: arrays keep their element type at runtime (String[] knows it is String[]), generics do not; List<?> and raw List are the only reifiable list types

chapters.title: Consequences of Erasure
points: Illegal with type parameters: new T(), new T[10], T.class, static T field, and catch/throw of T
instanceof List<String> does not compile; use instanceof List<?> or a plain List check
Overloads that differ only by type argument clash: void f(List<String>) and void f(List<Integer>) have the same erasure, so compile error
Workaround for runtime type: pass a Class<T> token (Class<T> c; c.cast(o), c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()) or capture with an anonymous subclass (TypeToken pattern)
Unchecked cast (T) obj compiles with a warning and never fails inside the generic code; the ClassCastException surfaces later in the caller

chapters.title: Raw Types and Generic Arrays
points: Raw type: using List with no argument turns off generic checking for that use; only exists for legacy compatibility, so never write it in new code
Raw to generic assignment List<String> l = new ArrayList(); gives an unchecked warning; add(42) through a raw reference compiles and corrupts the list
Generic array creation new List<String>[3] is illegal because arrays check element type at runtime and erasure can't; use List<List<String>> or new ArrayList<?>[3] with a cast
Generic varargs <T> void f(T... a) builds a T[] and triggers a heap pollution warning; @SafeVarargs on final/static/private methods is allowed only if you don't write into or expose the array
(T[]) new Object[n] inside a generic class works but leaks ClassCastException if the array is returned as T[]; prefer ArrayList<T> or Array.newInstance(cls, n)

chapters.title: Generics Cheat Sheet
points: Declare: class Box<T>, <T extends A & B> bound, static <T> R m(...) generic method; no primitives, use wrappers
Wildcards: ? read as Object; ? extends T read-only producer; ? super T write-only consumer; PECS decides
Invariance: List<Integer> is not a List<Number>; use List<? extends Number> to accept both
Erasure bans: new T(), new T[], T.class, instanceof List<String>, static T field, overloads differing only by type argument
Fixes: Class<T> token, @SafeVarargs, List<T> instead of T[]; avoid raw types and suppress unchecked warnings only when proven safe
